title: Reshape tables
goal: Move between long and wide layouts and choose when to aggregate.
prerequisites: Understand keys, groups, and summary functions.

cells.title: Melt wide columns into rows
cells.explanation: A wide table stores different measures in different columns. melt turns selected measure columns into a label column and a value column. The ID is repeated so every new row still belongs to a student.
cells.code:
wide = students().head(3)[["Student_ID", "Score", "Attendance"]]
result = wide.melt(id_vars="Student_ID", value_vars=["Score", "Attendance"], var_name="Measure", value_name="Value")
print(result)

questions.prompt: Which column stays as an identifier?
How many long rows will 3 students and 2 measures produce?
Are Score and Attendance being added together?
questions.answer: No. melt changes the layout; the values remain separate and their measure labels are retained.

cells.task: Use the first four students and melt Score and Study_Hours instead.
cells.hint: Change head(3) to head(4) and the two measure names.
cells.solution:
wide = students().head(4)[["Student_ID", "Score", "Study_Hours"]]
result = wide.melt(id_vars="Student_ID", var_name="Measure", value_name="Value")
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Four students with two measures produce eight rows.

check.feedback: melt reorganizes values into a long layout without aggregating them.

cells.watch: A shared Value column may contain measures with different units; keep and use Measure.
cells.takeaway: Long form keeps one measured value per row.

cells.title: Pivot a unique pair
cells.explanation: pivot moves distinct category labels into columns. Every index-and-column pair must identify at most one value. Here each student has one Score and one Attendance value.
cells.code:
long = students().head(3).melt(id_vars="Student_ID", value_vars=["Score", "Attendance"], var_name="Measure", value_name="Value")
result = long.pivot(index="Student_ID", columns="Measure", values="Value")
print(result)

questions.prompt: Which labels become the output columns?
questions.answer: The distinct Measure values: Attendance and Score.

questions.prompt: What is the Score for S002 after pivoting?
Why can repeated Student_ID and Measure pairs cause an error?
questions.answer: pivot cannot choose which of several values belongs in the same output cell.

cells.task: Pivot the same long table so Measure labels form the rows and Student_ID labels form the columns.
cells.hint: Exchange the arguments assigned to index and columns.
cells.solution:
long = students().head(3).melt(id_vars="Student_ID", value_vars=["Score", "Attendance"], var_name="Measure", value_name="Value")
result = long.pivot(index="Measure", columns="Student_ID", values="Value")
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The values stay the same, but the two table axes exchange roles.

check.prompt: What must be unique for pivot?
check.feedback: The pair identifies one output cell and must have a single value.

cells.watch: Use pivot_table only when you actually intend to aggregate repeated pairs.

cells.title: Aggregate with pivot_table
cells.explanation: Several students share the same Campus and Program. pivot_table can reduce those repeated combinations using an explicit aggregation function. Naming aggfunc makes the summary rule clear.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = df.pivot_table(index="Campus", columns="Program", values="Score", aggfunc="mean", observed=True)
print(result.round(2))

questions.answer: The mean Score of students with that Campus and Program.

questions.prompt: How many campus-by-program cells are there?
questions.answer: Four: two campuses times two programs.
It documents the statistic; mean, sum, and count answer different questions.

cells.task: Change the table to count Student_ID records for each campus and program.
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = df.pivot_table(index="Campus", columns="Program", values="Student_ID", aggfunc="count", observed=True)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The counts are Dubai AI 2, Dubai IT 4, RAK AI 4, and RAK IT 2.

check.prompt: Which method handles repeated pairs by summarizing them?
check.feedback: pivot_table applies an aggregation to values sharing the same output cell.

cells.verify:
assert result.shape == (2, 2)
assert result.loc["Dubai", "AI"] == 92
assert result.loc["RAK", "IT"] == 77.5
cells.watch: Filling an absent combination with zero implies a meaning; it is not automatically appropriate for a mean.
cells.takeaway: Choose an aggregation that matches the question.

cells.title: Count combinations with crosstab
cells.explanation: crosstab counts how often two categories occur together. normalize="index" instead reports proportions within each row. The denominator changes, so always label the result.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = pd.crosstab(df["Campus"], df["Program"])
print(result)

questions.prompt: What is counted in each cell?
questions.answer: Students in that Campus and Program combination.

questions.prompt: How many RAK students are in AI?
Would a larger count alone prove a stronger preference?
questions.answer: No. Group sizes matter; proportions may be more suitable for that question.

cells.task: Calculate program percentages within each campus and keep the unrounded percentages in result. Print a version rounded to one decimal place.
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = pd.crosstab(df["Campus"], df["Program"], normalize="index") * 100
print(result.round(1))
cells.solution_note: Each campus row sums to 100%. AI accounts for about 66.7% in RAK and 33.3% in Dubai in this fictional table.

check.feedback: Each cell is divided by its own row total.

cells.watch: Say whether percentages are by row, by column, or of the whole table.
cells.takeaway: Counts and proportions answer different questions.
